newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain heightens security to combat violence surge.
newsitem.headline: Spain heightens security to combat violence surge.

text.p: Spain has ordered increased police patrols in major cities, more security for judges, politicians and military figures and is seeking help from citizens to combat a wave of violence blamed on Basque separatists.
Official sources told Reuters on Wednesday the decision was made at a high-level meeting of police, civil guard and intelligence agents at the Interior Ministry on Tuesday.

"Police presence in the streets of some cities will be increased," a government source said. Madrid, Barcelona, the southern region of Andalusia and the northern Navarra region were among areas targeted for heightened security.
Growing violence which culminated in three killings this week has forced the 29-year-old conflict with the violent ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) back to the top of the government's agenda.
Officials were bracing for a worsening of violence.
"Possibly harder days are still to come," Conservative Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said on Tuesday.
ETA is suspected in five killings so far this year. About 800 people have been killed since the group's drive for independence began in 1968.
On Monday, a gunman fatally shot a Supreme Court judge in the head in Madrid only hours after a car bomb killed a hairdresser going to work at a military base in the southern city of Granada.
On Tuesday, a local businessman was shot in the head during carnival celebrations in the Basque town of Tolosa and died.

A top priority for security forces is cracking two ETA cells which they suspect in recent attacks -- "Comando Madrid" which is active in the Spanish capital and "Comando Donosti" which operates in the Basque country.
Efforts are also being concentrated on uncovering two independent cells holding two hostages, official sources said.
Police are appealing for help from witnesses of attacks.
Despite media reports that Basque residents are reluctant to serve as jurors in ETA cases, one government source said there is no concern about intimidation of potential witnesses.
"There is no problem. All the information is anonymous," one source said.

Concerns about intimidation were raised by a killing of a bicycle vendor in the Basque city of San Sebastian at the end of January. Newspaper reports said ETA may have suspected the vendor of turning in one of its activists who had visited the bicycle shop hours before his arrest.

Though ETA has not claimed responsibilty for any of the attacks this week, some observers speculated the resurgence of violence may be motivated by growing sense of frustration at the nine-month-old government's refusal to negotiate with ETA.
The attacks have hardened the government's position against talks unless ETA quits violence and releases the hostages.
The timing of the attacks suggested they may also be linked to a Supreme Court summons of the 25-member leadership of ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna (HB).

The leaders were to appear in court this month on charges of distributing a pro-ETA video in last year's election campaign and one member of the group warned publicly last week that Spain would pay the price for the court's action.
One of the summoned HB leaders was found dead at his family home on Monday from an apparent suicide.
At the weekend, a suspected ETA activist awaiting trial in jail in a separate case was found hanged in his cell with hands and feet bound in what the government said was suicide.
